Growth rates, tables and plots

growth-and-reporting.Rmd

A forecast is a set of levels, such as thousands of jobs in each quarter. Readers mostly want to know how fast things change, so reports show growth rates, comparisons with a year earlier and indexes alongside the levels. This article covers the functions that compute those (growth rates, period-to-date totals, indexes) and those that show them (tables and interactive plots). The examples use the package’s Hawaii data: payroll jobs (quarterly) and visitor arrivals (monthly and daily).

library(fcutils)
options(
  fcutils.bnk_start = as.Date("1998-01-01"),
  fcutils.bnk_end = as.Date("2035-12-31")
)
q <- conv_xts(quarterly_data_example)
jobs <- q$E_NF_HI

Growth rates

pcmp(x, lag, comp_freq) (percent change, compounded) is the average growth per period over the last lag periods, compounded comp_freq times. With comp_freq = 4, quarterly growth becomes an annual rate, so pcmp(x, 4, 4) is the growth over a year. One function covers the usual measures for a quarterly series:

gr <- tsbox::ts_c(
  q_q = pcmp(jobs, lag = 1),                     # quarter on quarter
  q_q_ann = pcmp(jobs, lag = 1, comp_freq = 4),  # annualized
  y_y = pcmp(jobs, lag = 4, comp_freq = 4),      # year on year
  ten_yr_ann = pcmp(jobs, lag = 40, comp_freq = 4)  # average over 10 years
)
round(tail(gr, 2), 2)
#>             q_q q_q_ann  y_y ten_yr_ann
#> 2024-10-01 0.55    2.22 1.81       0.18
#> 2025-01-01 0.72    2.92 1.73       0.21

pc_to_pca() and pca_to_pc() convert between period and annualized rates, and cagr() gives the compound annual growth rate between the first and last observation, in percent, with the years elapsed:

cagr(jobs[p(2015, 2024)])
#> # A tibble: 1 × 2
#>   years_elapsed E_NF_HI
#>           <dbl>   <dbl>
#> 1          9.75   0.142

ma(x, order) is a trailing moving average that includes the current period: ma(x, 4) averages each quarter with the three before it.

Series of different size are hard to compare as levels. Total jobs are about six times accommodation and food services jobs. index_to_base(x, base_per) divides each series by its value in a base period and multiplies by 100. Both series then equal 100 in the base period, and the index shows the percent above or below the base. With one date, the first period on or after it is the base. With two dates, the average over that span is set to 100, so c(2019.1, 2019.4) takes the 2019 average as the base. Here the two series against 2019, through the 2020 pandemic:

idx <- index_to_base(q[, c("E_NF_HI", "EAF_HI")], c(2019.1, 2019.4))
round(idx[p(2019.4, 2020.3)], 1)
#>            E_NF_HI EAF_HI
#> 2019-10-01   100.3  100.0
#> 2020-01-01   100.3  100.3
#> 2020-04-01    78.1   45.8
#> 2020-07-01    79.4   45.1

Period to date

Monthly and daily data that are not seasonally adjusted, such as visitor arrivals, rise and fall with the seasons. Comparing March with February mixes seasonal swings with real change. A common fix is to compare the months of this year so far with the same months a year earlier. The to-date functions do this. They accumulate within a year, fiscal year (July to June), quarter or month, and compare with the same span a year earlier.

Function Period Returns
ytd_agg(x, avg) calendar year average (or sum, avg = FALSE) so far
ytd_gr(x) calendar year % change of the year so far on a year earlier
fytd_agg(), fytd_gr() fiscal year the same for the fiscal year
mtd_agg(), mtd_gr() month the same within each month, for daily data
ptd_agg(x, per), ptd_gr(x, per) per: “year”, “quarter”, “month”, “week”, “day” the general form

Visitor arrivals in early 2025:

vis <- conv_xts(monthly_data_example)$VISNS_HI
round(tail(tsbox::ts_c(
  arrivals = vis,
  ytd_avg = ytd_agg(vis),
  ytd_sum = ytd_agg(vis, avg = FALSE),
  ytd_gr = ytd_gr(vis),
  fytd_gr = fytd_gr(vis)
), 4), 1)
#>            arrivals ytd_avg ytd_sum ytd_gr fytd_gr
#> 2024-12-01    910.1   809.3  9711.4    0.6     4.6
#> 2025-01-01    792.2   792.2   792.2    3.8     4.5
#> 2025-02-01    759.7   775.9  1551.9    1.0     3.8
#> 2025-03-01    903.9   818.6  2455.7    1.7     3.7

In March, ytd_avg is the average of January to March and ytd_sum their total. The year to March 2025 is 1.7% above the same months of 2024. The fiscal year to March, which started in July 2024, is 3.7% above July 2023 to March 2024.

The month-to-date functions do the same with daily data within each month. Daily visitor arrivals in March 2022, as travel recovered from the pandemic:

vis_d <- conv_xts(daily_data_example)$VISPNS_HI
round(tail(tsbox::ts_c(
  arrivals = vis_d,
  mtd_avg = mtd_agg(vis_d),
  mtd_gr = mtd_gr(vis_d)
), 3), 1)
#>            arrivals mtd_avg mtd_gr
#> 2022-03-23    22693 22627.0   86.5
#> 2022-03-24    25682 22754.3   85.5
#> 2022-03-25    25556 22866.4   82.9

The first 25 days of March 2022 averaged 22,866 arrivals a day, 83% more than the first 25 days of March 2021.

A quarter in progress

agg() leaves out a quarter until all three of its months are published. A forecast often needs the current quarter sooner. partial estimates the last quarter of each series from the months published so far: "average" takes their mean, and "growth" grows an earlier complete quarter by the change from the same months of that quarter. By default "growth" looks back one quarter; partial_lag = "1 year" compares with the same months a year earlier, which suits data that are not seasonally adjusted.

Suppose visitor arrivals were published only through February 2025:

vis_feb <- head(vis, -1)
q1 <- tsbox::ts_c(
  drop = agg(vis_feb, target_freq = "quarter"),
  average = agg(vis_feb, target_freq = "quarter", partial = "average"),
  growth = agg(vis_feb, target_freq = "quarter", partial = "growth"),
  growth_1y = agg(vis_feb, target_freq = "quarter", partial = "growth",
                  partial_lag = "1 year"),
  actual = agg(vis, target_freq = "quarter")
)
round(tail(q1, 2), 1)
#>             drop average growth growth_1y actual
#> 2024-10-01 818.5   818.5  818.5     818.5  818.5
#> 2025-01-01    NA   775.9  821.9     812.9  818.6

With March published, the 2025Q1 average is 818.6. The mean of January and February misses the March peak and comes in at 775.9. Growing 2024Q4 by the change from October–November to January–February gives 821.9, and growing 2024Q1 by the change from January–February 2024 gives 812.9. For a rate, such as the unemployment rate, "average" is the usual choice.

Tables

gen_table() lays out series with their growth rates. By default the dates run across and each series and growth rate has a row; time_across = FALSE turns that around, which suits a short page. percent picks the growth rate shown with each series: "pc" (period on period), "pcy" (year on year), "pca" (annualized) or "none".

gen_table(q[, c("E_NF_HI", "EAF_HI")],
  tbl_start = "2024-01-01", tbl_end = "2025-01-01", percent = "pcy",
  time_across = FALSE
)
#> # A tibble: 5 × 5
#>   time       EAF_HI `EAF_HI (YoY%)` E_NF_HI `E_NF_HI (YoY%)`
#>   <date>      <dbl>           <dbl>   <dbl>            <dbl>
#> 1 2024-01-01   106.            0.66    637.             0.89
#> 2 2024-04-01   106.           -0.27    636.             0.43
#> 3 2024-07-01   106.            1.13    640.             1.19
#> 4 2024-10-01   107.            2.66    643.             1.81
#> 5 2025-01-01   108.            1.7     648.             1.73

With save_loc, it writes the table to a CSV file or, for .html, to a searchable page.

Interactive plots

The plot functions draw dygraphs: hover to read values, drag to zoom, and use the range selector at the bottom. rng_start and rng_end set the initial window. All plots on a page zoom together, so a page of plots keeps one date window; the two plots below share 2016 to 2028.

plot_fc() shows up to three series, typically the forecast, an earlier forecast and history, as lines, with the growth of the first as bars on the right axis and a table below. This is the jobs forecast from Building a forecast against history:

jobs_fc <- extend(jobs, 2025.4 ~ 1.2, 2027.4 ~ 0.8, type = "growth")
plot_fc(
  tsbox::ts_c(forecast = jobs_fc, history = jobs),
  rng_start = "2016-01-01", rng_end = "2028-01-01",
  table_start = "2024-01-01", table_end = "2028-01-01",
  width = 700
)

rate = TRUE shows the change in points instead of the percent change, for rates such as the unemployment rate, and yoy_gr = FALSE shows growth on the previous period instead of year on year.

plot_1() plots one or more series with the growth of the first, and plot_2ax() puts the first series on the left axis and the rest on the right. plot_comp_2() shows several series in two panels, levels and growth. plot_comp_3() adds a panel with each series indexed to 1 at base_date, which compares series of different size. Accommodation and food services jobs fell much further in 2020 than total jobs:

plot_comp_3(q[, c("E_NF_HI", "EAF_HI")],
  base_date = "2019-10-01",
  rng_start = "2016-01-01", rng_end = "2028-01-01", width = 700
)

To collect many plots on one page that can be shared as a single file, put them in a list and pass it to save_plot_list().
